summary: Eric Allam frames the talk around a fundamental shift agents pose to backend infrastructure: moving from 30 years of stateless compute to stateful compute. He begins with a history lesson. CGI (1993) forked a new process per HTTP request—completely stateless. PHP and the LAMP stack reused processes but kept the principle that request plus database state equals response, known as the shared-nothing architecture. Everything since—Rails, Node.js, serverless—follows this paradigm. As web apps grew more sophisticated, multi-step async side effects emerged (e.g., process order: charge card, send receipt), creating failure-handling problems. Workflow and durable execution engines solved this 10–15 years ago via the replay model: wrap each side effect in a cached step, skip completed steps on retry. This builds durable execution on top of stateless compute and yields an audit trail, but imposes rigid code structure and requires determinism. When LLMs arrived circa 2023, they initially fit as another workflow step, but tool calling introduced the agent loop where the LLM orchestrates code rather than code orchestrating the LLM. Applying replay to agent loops, every LLM call and tool call becomes a journal entry; the journal grows with each turn until hitting fundamental limits. Allam notes agent work capacity is doubling every 4–7 months, currently a few hours, heading toward days. He argues agents are sessions, not transactions. He then separates durability into two halves: context durability (system messages, tool calls, responses—an append-only log already handled by databases, object storage, or distributed file systems) and execution durability (cloned repos, installed packages, in-memory datasets, dev servers, sandboxed subprocesses—state in the compute layer that cannot be recreated from a log). For execution durability, he proposes snapshot and restore, a concept dating to IBM mainframes in 1966 and CRIU in 2011. Trigger.dev shipped CRIU-based snapshots in 2024 with millions of snapshot restores, but CRIU has limitations: it only checkpoints a single process (not subprocesses like FFmpeg or Chrome), only captures open files, and container compatibility introduces slow registry push/pull. They then moved to Firecracker microVMs to snapshot entire machines. A naive 512MB VM produces a 512MB snapshot, so they applied seekable compression—decompressing only needed memory pages at restore time—plus layering techniques, achieving 14MB compressed snapshots with sub-second save and couple-hundred-millisecond restore. They benchmark 15,000 VM starts per minute. All of this is bundled into FC Run, an open-source Docker-like CLI for Firecracker VMs. Allam concludes that combining context logs with execution snapshots yields durability across versions, turns, and failures, pointing toward a future of stateful compute.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Agents are forcing a shift from 30 years of stateless compute to stateful compute with snapshot and restore at its core.
The replay model works for bounded multi-step workflows but breaks down for long-running agent sessions where the journal grows unboundedly.
Agent durability has two separable halves: context durability (append-only log of LLM I/O) and execution durability (compute-layer state).
Execution durability requires OS-level snapshot and restore rather than smarter logging; context durability is already solved by databases and object storage.
CRIU works for single-process snapshots but fails for multi-process workloads (FFmpeg, Chrome), only captures open files, and is slow with container registries.
Firecracker microVMs enable full-machine snapshot and restore, picking up exactly where the VM left off.
Seekable compression and layering reduce 512MB VM snapshots to 14MB compressed, with sub-second save and hundred-millisecond restore times.
Trigger.dev benchmarks 15,000 Firecracker VM starts per minute using FC Run, an upcoming open-source Docker-like CLI.
Combining context logs with execution snapshots achieves durability across versions, turns, and failures for agent sessions.
Checkpoint and restore is not new—IBM mainframes had it in 1966 and CRIU provided process-level suspend/restore in 2011.

sections.title: Introduction and the Agent Problem
sections.summary: Eric Allam introduces himself as co-founder of Trigger.dev and frames the talk: agents work on local machines but deploying them to production requires long-running, durable, error-recoverable execution. He positions the talk around the fundamental shift agents pose to backend infrastructure.

sections.title: History: CGI, LAMP, and Shared Nothing Architecture
sections.summary: Traces backend history from CGI (1993) through PHP/LAMP to the shared-nothing architecture where compute is stateless and state lives in the database. This paradigm dominated backend infrastructure for 30 years, including Rails, Node.js, and serverless.

sections.title: Side Effects and the Replay Model
sections.summary: Explains how multi-step async side effects created failure-handling problems (e.g., double-charging a credit card). Workflow and durable execution engines solved this 10–15 years ago via the replay model: wrap each side effect in a cached step, skip completed steps on retry. Downsides include rigid code structure, required determinism, and tricky journal versioning.

sections.title: LLMs, Tool Calling, and the Agent Loop
sections.summary: LLMs initially fit as workflow steps, but tool calling introduced the agent loop where the LLM orchestrates code. Applying replay to agent loops makes every LLM call and tool call a journal entry; the journal grows unboundedly. Agent work capacity is doubling every 4–7 months. Agents are sessions, not transactions—they run as long as the user wants.

sections.title: Two Halves of Agent Durability
sections.summary: Separates agent durability into context durability (system messages, tool calls, responses—an append-only log already handled by databases, object storage, or distributed file systems, enabling cross-version durability) and execution durability (cloned repos, installed packages, in-memory datasets, dev servers, subprocesses—compute-layer state that cannot be recreated from a log).

sections.title: Snapshot and Restore: The Solution and Its Precedents
sections.summary: Proposes OS-level snapshot and restore for execution durability: snapshot the machine, shut it down, restore on next user message. Enables cheap durability across turns and flexible error recovery. Observes this concept is not new—IBM mainframes had checkpoint/restore in 1966, and CRIU enabled process suspend/restore from user space in 2011. Agents are forcing the shift from stateless to stateful compute.

sections.title: From CRIU to Firecracker: Building Production Snapshot/Restore
sections.summary: Details Trigger.dev's implementation journey. CRIU works by injecting a process like a parasite, dumping memory, then removing traces—transparent to the process and container-compatible. Shipped in 2024 with millions of snapshot restores since. CRIU limitations: only checkpoints a single process (fails for FFmpeg/Chrome), only captures open files, and container registry push/pull is slow. Moved to Firecracker microVMs to snapshot entire machines. Naive 512MB VM snapshots are 512MB on disk, so they applied seekable compression (decompressing only needed pages at restore time) and layering, achieving 14MB compressed snapshots. Performance: snapshots slightly under one second, restores a couple hundred milliseconds. Benchmarks show 15,000 VM starts per minute. All bundled into FC Run, an upcoming open-source Docker-like CLI for Firecracker VMs. Concludes that context logs plus execution snapshots yield durability across versions, turns, and failures—pointing toward a future of stateful compute.
